sections.h: 1 Esdras 6-9: from the rebuilding to the reading of the law
sections.b:
The last four chapters of 1 Esdras retell Ezra 5:1-10:44 and Nehemiah 7:73-8:12 in one continuous story. Darius confirms Cyrus's decree and the temple is finished and dedicated (1 Esdras 6:1-7:15); Ezra comes from Babylon with Artaxerxes' letter (1 Esdras 8:1-64); he hears of the mixed marriages, prays, and the foreign wives are sent away with their children (1 Esdras 8:65-9:36); and he reads the law to all the people (1 Esdras 9:37-55). There is no Nehemiah: his title becomes a man called Attarates (1 Esdras 9:49), and Ezra himself is called "high priest" (1 Esdras 9:40). The Greek adds Zerubbabel to Darius's decree (1 Esdras 6:26-28), changes many names and numbers, and uses Greek-era terms such as Coele-Syria and the king's "Friends." It ends in mid-scene: "And they gathered together" (1 Esdras 9:55). Josephus follows its order, sets the reading of the law at the Feast of Tabernacles, and ends with Ezra's death (Antiquities 11.154-158).

Note on numbers: this site cites 1 Esdras in the verse numbers of Swete's Greek text, which in these chapters run behind the KJV's: Ezra's prayer, for example, is 1 Esdras 8:71-87 here and 8:74-90 in the KJV.

common: 1 Esdras 6-9 follows Ezra 5-10 and Nehemiah 8 closely, with many small changes of name, number and wording.
Bullard and Hatton's handbook calls the book's last sentence (1 Esdras 9:55) "only a fragment" and thinks the book once had more.
uncommon: Josephus, who follows 1 Esdras, sets Ezra in the reign of Xerxes, not Artaxerxes (Antiquities 11.120-121).

claude.title: Claude's reading: a book about knowing the law
claude.body: 1 Esdras twice calls the people's sin agnoia, "error, ignorance" (1 Esdras 8:72; 9:20), and it ends with the law read aloud and taught to all the people (1 Esdras 9:37-55). Read together, the last chapters move from sin done without knowing, through confession, to a people who know the law. This is my own suggestion.

sections.b: 1 Esdras gives Ezra a larger role than the Hebrew books. With no Nehemiah in the story, Ezra alone leads the reform and the reading of the law. He is "gifted" in Moses' law and has "great knowledge" (1 Esdras 8:3, 8:7); he wears a "holy robe" (1 Esdras 8:68); the king's letter calls him "reader of the law" (anagnostes, 1 Esdras 8:8-9); and at the reading he is "the high priest" (1 Esdras 9:40, 9:49). Josephus, who follows 1 Esdras, sets Ezra under Xerxes and ends his story with his death and burial in Jerusalem (Antiquities 11.120-121; 11.158). A teaching in the Babylonian Talmud says Ezra was worthy for the Torah to be given through him had Moses not come first (Sanhedrin 21b).

Where Ezra 5-6 keeps Zerubbabel in the background, 1 Esdras writes him into the documents. The vessels are handed "to Zerubbabel and to Sanabassar the governor" (1 Esdras 6:17), and Darius's order names "Zerubbabel, the Lord's servant and deputy governor of Judea" and pays the allowance "to Zerubbabel the governor" (1 Esdras 6:26-28). The title "the Lord's servant" echoes Haggai 2:23. The changes fit 1 Esdras's story of Zerubbabel as the wise young guard who won Darius's favor (1 Esdras 4:13-57).

sections.b: 1 Esdras calls Sheshbazzar Sanabassar and has the vessels given to both him and Zerubbabel (1 Esdras 6:17), yet only Sanabassar lays the foundation (1 Esdras 6:19). The pairing keeps the two men distinct and suggests that Zerubbabel's name was added to a sentence about Sheshbazzar alone (compare Ezra 5:14-16).

1 Esdras tells the marriage reform of Ezra 9-10 with several changes. Its list of peoples has Edomites and no Ammonites (1 Esdras 8:66). The sin is "lawlessness" and "error" rather than unfaithfulness and guilt (1 Esdras 8:67, 8:72). The four men who oppose the plan in Ezra 10:15 help to carry it out (1 Esdras 9:14). And where Ezra 10:44 ends with a hard sentence, 1 Esdras says plainly, "they sent them away with their children" (1 Esdras 9:36), as Josephus also does (Antiquities 11.152). Even the Passover of 1 Esdras 7:13 has no outsiders who join the exiles, unlike Ezra 6:21.

sections.h: The law read and taught to the people
sections.b: 1 Esdras ends with Ezra reading the law to all the people before the temple's east gate, from a wooden platform (1 Esdras 9:37-55). Where Nehemiah 8:8 and 8:12 speak of explaining and understanding, the Greek uses a rare verb, perhaps "inspire," for what the Levites did with the reading and what the words did to the people (1 Esdras 9:48; 9:55; the KJV has "understand"). Earlier the king's letter makes the law royal law for the Jews of Syria and Phoenicia, with Ezra to appoint judges and teach it (1 Esdras 8:23-24).

sections.h: The feast 1 Esdras does not reach
sections.b: In Nehemiah the reading of the law leads the next day to the discovery of the Feast of Booths (Nehemiah 8:13-18). 1 Esdras stops just before it, with "And they gathered together" (1 Esdras 9:55). Josephus, who follows 1 Esdras, places Ezra's reading at the Feast of Tabernacles and tells of eight days in booths (Antiquities 11.154-157).

Ezra's confession in 1 Esdras 8:71-87 follows Ezra 9:6-15 but changes its images: the remnant is "a root and a name," the sins are "errors," and God is "true" rather than "in the right." The people answer with weeping, an oath and the sending away of foreign wives, then with joy at the reading of the law (1 Esdras 8:88-9:55).

1 Esdras dates the completion of the rebuilt temple to the twenty-third of Adar in Darius's sixth year, where Ezra 6:15 has the third (1 Esdras 7:5). The dedication offerings, twelve goats for the twelve tribes, and the Passover that follows match Ezra 6:16-22 (1 Esdras 7:6-15).

1 Esdras tells the reading of the law of Nehemiah 8 but has no Nehemiah. Where Nehemiah 8:9 has "Nehemiah, who was the governor," the Greek has a man named Attarates, from the Persian title tirshata (1 Esdras 9:49). Since 1 Esdras leaves out all of Nehemiah's memoir, the missing name does not show that the Hebrew once lacked it.

1 Esdras often uses "the Most High God" where Ezra's Aramaic has "the God of the heavens" (1 Esdras 6:30; 8:19; 8:21), and at the reading of the law it has "the Most High God, the Almighty" (1 Esdras 9:46). These Greek titles were familiar to Jews in the Greek-speaking world.
